# 🏗️ What is `tidymodels`?

## What is [`tidymodels`](https://www.tidymodels.org/)?

A **meta-package** for modeling and machine learning that shares the design philosophy, grammar, and data structures of the `tidyverse`.

**Built by:**

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
![](img/kuhn.png){.small width=50%}

**Max Kuhn** — author of `caret`, the original R ML package.
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
![](img/julia.png){.small width=50%}

**Julia Silge** — engineer, blogger, and the most active tidymodels evangelist.
:::
:::

# 🤔 Why bother?

## R has 200+ ML packages and they all speak different languages 😩

::: {.incremental}
- I ❤️ R, but…
- My 🤯 with the **idiosyncratic syntax** developed for every model algorithm.
:::

::: {.fragment}
```r
# Linear regression
lm_fit    <- lm(y ~ ., data = df)
glm_fit   <- glm(y ~ ., data = df, family = gaussian)
caret_fit <- train(y ~ ., data = df, method = "lm")
```

> Same model. Three packages. Three syntaxes. 🤬
:::

---

## Same model, different packages

The same problem persists for **Random Forest**:

::: {.panel-tabset}

### `randomForest`
- **Number of predictors:** `mtry`
- **Number of trees:** `ntree`
- **Number of splits:** `nodesize`

### `ranger`
- **Number of predictors:** `mtry`
- **Number of trees:** `num.trees`
- **Number of splits:** `min.node.size`

### `sparklyr`
- **Number of predictors:** `feature_subset_strategy`
- **Number of trees:** `num_trees`
- **Number of splits:** `min_instances_per_node`

:::

::: {.fragment}
> Three packages. Three names for **the exact same hyperparameter**. 🤯
:::

::: {.footer}
[ML with Tidymodels](https://simonschoe.github.io/ml-with-tidymodels/#1)
:::

---

## `tidymodels` solves this with `parsnip` 😎

**One unified syntax** for every model:

```r
# Logistic Regression
logistic_reg() |>
  set_engine("glm") |>
  set_mode("classification")

# Random Forest — same shape!
rand_forest(mtry = tune(), trees = 500) |>
  set_engine("ranger") |>
  set_mode("classification")

# XGBoost — same shape!
boost_tree(trees = 1000, learn_rate = tune()) |>
  set_engine("xgboost") |>
  set_mode("classification")
```

::: {.fragment}
> Learn one pattern → use **238+ models**. 🚀
:::

---

## The `tidymodels` ecosystem 🧱

| Package | What it does | Day you'll use it |
|---------|-------------|-------------------|
| 📦 **`rsample`** | Split data + create CV folds | Today |
| 🍳 **`recipes`** | Preprocess (impute, normalize, dummy…) | Today |
| 🌱 **`parsnip`** | Specify the model | Today |
| 🔗 **`workflows`** | Bundle recipe + model | Today |
| 📏 **`yardstick`** | Compute metrics (accuracy, ROC AUC…) | Today |
| 🎛️ **`tune` + `dials`** | Hyperparameter tuning | Tomorrow |
| 🧹 **`broom`** | Tidy model output (`tidy()`, `glance()`) | Today |

::: {.fragment}
**Loading them all at once:**

```r
library(tidymodels)
```
:::

# 🗺️ The ML Pipeline

## The 7 steps you'll repeat for *every* model

::: {.incremental}
1. **Split** the data into train / test.
2. **Recipe** — describe the preprocessing.
3. **Spec** — choose the model and engine.
4. **Workflow** — bundle the recipe and the spec.
5. **Fit** the workflow on the training set.
6. **Predict** on the test set.
7. **Evaluate** with metrics (accuracy, ROC AUC…).
:::

::: {.fragment}
::: {.callout-tip}
## The good news
This is *literally the same code* for Lasso, Decision Trees, Random Forest, KNN, and XGBoost. **Only the spec changes.** ✨
:::
:::

# 📚 Quick Review: Logistic Regression

## What is logistic regression?

::: {.fragment}
**Logistic regression…**

::: {.incremental}
- Is a **supervised learning** algorithm used to *classify data* into categories by **predicting the probability** that an observation belongs to a particular class, based on its features.
- Is most often used for **binary classification** — deciding between two groups (Yes / No, Survived / Died, Carried weapon / Did not).
- Outputs a number between 0 and 1 that we interpret as a **probability**, then threshold (usually at 0.5) to assign a class.
:::
:::

::: {.fragment}
> 🧠 **Why start with logistic regression?** It's the simplest and most interpretable classifier — every fancier model (Lasso, trees, RF, KNN) is judged against it.
:::

# 🎬 A Real Example

## Research question

> **Can we predict whether an adolescent will carry a weapon to school based on other risk behaviors reported in the YRBS?**

::: {.incremental}
- **Outcome**: `WeaponCarrying` (binary: Yes / No)
- **Predictors**: All other risk behavior items in the survey
- **Why it matters**: Identifying patterns of risk could help target school-based prevention.
:::

---

## The data — `MLearnYRBSS::riskyBehaviors`

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false
library(tidymodels)
library(MLearnYRBSS)
library(janitor)
library(skimr)

data("riskyBehaviors")
glimpse(riskyBehaviors)
```

---

## Setup — load packages

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false
# pak::pak("tidymodels")        # if not installed
# pak::pak("MLearnYRBSS")       # for the dataset

library(tidymodels)
library(MLearnYRBSS)
library(janitor)
```

::: {.fragment}
::: {.callout-note}
## What `library(tidymodels)` loads
A whole family of packages: `rsample`, `recipes`, `parsnip`, `workflows`, `tune`, `dials`, `yardstick`, `broom`, plus `dplyr`, `ggplot2`, `tibble`, `purrr`. Almost everything you need for ML.
:::
:::

---

## Recode the outcome to binary

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| output-location: fragment
analysis_data <-
    riskyBehaviors |>
    mutate(
        WeaponCarryingSchool = case_when(
            WeaponCarrying == 1 ~ "No",
            WeaponCarrying %in% c(2, 3, 4, 5) ~ "Yes",
            .default = NA_character_
        ),
        WeaponCarryingSchool = factor(WeaponCarryingSchool)
    ) |>
    drop_na(WeaponCarryingSchool) |>
    select(-WeaponCarrying)

analysis_data |> count(WeaponCarryingSchool)
```

::: {.fragment}
::: {.callout-warning}
## Class imbalance ⚖️
About **8% Yes vs 92% No**. We'll handle this with `strata =` in the split (and later, downsampling for tuning). Always look at this *before* modeling.
:::
:::

# 1️⃣ Split: train + test

## Why split FIRST?

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
::: {.incremental}
- If you train *and* evaluate on the same data, your metrics are **inflated** — the model has memorized the answers.
- **The test set is sacred**: it's the *only* honest measure of how the model will perform on data it has never seen.
- **Split BEFORE you do anything else.** Even before EDA on the predictors.
:::
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
::: {.callout-warning}
## Common beginner mistake
Splitting *after* you've already imputed missing values, normalized predictors, or computed PCA on the full dataset. That's **data leakage**, and your test metrics become a lie.

✅ Tidymodels protects you from this when you wrap the recipe in a `workflow()`.
:::
:::
:::

---

## `initial_split()` — stratified

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| output-location: fragment
set.seed(1990)

analysis_split <-
    initial_split(
        analysis_data,
        prop = 0.75,
        strata = WeaponCarryingSchool # ⬅️ keeps class balance in both sets
    )

analysis_train <- training(analysis_split)
analysis_test <- testing(analysis_split)

analysis_split
```

::: {.fragment}
::: {.callout-tip}
## `set.seed()`
Splits are random. Setting a seed makes your work **reproducible** — you and your teacher get the exact same train/test split.
:::
:::

---

## Sanity check — class balance preserved

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| output-location: fragment
analysis_train |>
    tabyl(WeaponCarryingSchool) |>
    adorn_pct_formatting(0)

analysis_test |>
    tabyl(WeaponCarryingSchool) |>
    adorn_pct_formatting(0)
```

::: {.fragment}
> Both sets are ~8% / 92% — `strata =` did its job. ✅
:::

# 2️⃣ Recipe: preprocessing

## What is a `recipe`?

A **blueprint** of preprocessing steps that will be learned from the **training set** and *then* applied to test or new data.

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| code-line-numbers: "2|3|4|5|6|7|8"
weapon_recipe <-
    recipe(WeaponCarryingSchool ~ ., data = analysis_train) |>
    step_zv(all_predictors()) |> # drop zero-variance predictors
    step_impute_mode(all_nominal_predictors()) |> # fill NAs in categoricals with the mode
    step_impute_mean(all_numeric_predictors()) |> # fill NAs in numerics with the mean
    step_normalize(all_numeric_predictors()) |> # mean = 0, sd = 1 (helps KNN later)
    step_corr(all_numeric_predictors(), threshold = 0.7) |> # drop highly correlated predictors
    step_dummy(all_nominal_predictors()) # one-hot encode categoricals
```

::: {.fragment}
::: {.callout-tip}
## How do I know which steps to use?
- 📖 [The "Pre-processing methods" table](https://www.tmwr.org/pre-proc-table.html) tells you what *each model* needs.
- 🤖 The [`usemodels`](https://usemodels.tidymodels.org/) package writes a starter recipe for you.
:::
:::

---

## What we just told R to do

```
── Recipe ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
── Inputs 
Number of variables by role
outcome:    1
predictor: 19

── Operations 
• Zero variance filter on: all_predictors()
• Mode imputation for: all_nominal_predictors()
• Mean imputation for: all_numeric_predictors()
• Centering and scaling for: all_numeric_predictors()
• Correlation filter on: all_numeric_predictors()
• Dummy variables from: all_nominal_predictors()
```

::: {.fragment}
::: {.callout-warning}
## Nothing has been computed yet!
A recipe is a **plan**, not an action. R hasn't touched the data yet — it's just remembering what you want to do.
:::
:::

---

## (Optional) See what the recipe will produce

You can `prep()` the recipe (learn the parameters from training data) and `bake()` it (apply to a dataset) — useful for **debugging**:

```{r}
#| echo: true
weapon_recipe |>
    prep() |>
    bake(new_data = NULL) |> # NULL = use the training set
    glimpse()
```

::: {.fragment}
> 💡 **In practice**, you don't need to prep + bake by hand — `workflow()` does it for you. But it's a great way to inspect what's happening.
:::

# 3️⃣ Spec: choose the model

## `parsnip` — the model spec

A spec has **3 components**:

::: {.incremental}
1. **Type** — what kind of model? (`logistic_reg`, `decision_tree`, `rand_forest`…)
2. **Mode** — `"classification"` or `"regression"`?
3. **Engine** — which underlying R package implements it? (`"glm"`, `"ranger"`, `"xgboost"`…)
:::

::: {.fragment}
```{r}
#| echo: true
#| output-location: fragment
weapon_spec <-
    logistic_reg() |>
    set_mode("classification") |>
    set_engine("glm")

weapon_spec
```
:::

---

## Want help writing the spec?

The [`usemodels`](https://usemodels.tidymodels.org/) package writes a **starter scaffold** for the *more complex* models — Lasso, Random Forest, KNN, XGBoost…

```{r}
#| echo: true
library(usemodels)

# A scaffold for tomorrow's Lasso!
use_glmnet(WeaponCarryingSchool ~ ., data = analysis_train)
```

::: {.fragment}
::: {.callout-tip}
## When to reach for `usemodels`
- ✅ `use_glmnet()` — Lasso, Ridge, Elastic Net
- ✅ `use_ranger()` — Random Forest
- ✅ `use_xgboost()` — XGBoost
- ✅ `use_kknn()` — K-Nearest Neighbors

It writes the recipe, the spec, the workflow, and the tuning grid — copy-paste, adjust, you're done. ✨

For plain `glm` like today's example, the spec is so short you don't need a scaffold. 🤷‍♀️
:::
:::

# 4️⃣ Workflow: bundle them

## `workflow()` = recipe + spec

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| output-location: fragment
weapon_workflow <-
    workflow() |>
    add_recipe(weapon_recipe) |>
    add_model(weapon_spec)

weapon_workflow
```

::: {.fragment}
::: {.callout-tip}
## Why bundling matters
A `workflow` keeps the recipe and the model **glued together**. When you fit, predict, or resample, the recipe is **always applied to the right data at the right time** — no leakage. 🛡️
:::
:::

# 5️⃣ Fit: train on the training set

## Train the model

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| output-location: fragment
weapon_fit <-
    weapon_workflow |>
    fit(data = analysis_train)
```

::: {.fragment}
**Behind the scenes, tidymodels:**

1. ✅ Runs `prep()` on the recipe using `analysis_train`
2. ✅ Bakes the training data through the recipe
3. ✅ Trains the model on the baked data
:::

::: {.fragment}
> 💡 The recipe **never sees the test set**. That's how leakage is prevented.
:::

---

## Interpret coefficients with `tidy()`

```{r}
#| echo: true
tidy_model <-
    weapon_fit |>
    tidy(
        exponentiate = TRUE, # convert log-odds to odds ratios
        conf.int = TRUE,
        conf.level = 0.95
    ) |>
    mutate(p.value = scales::pvalue(p.value))

tidy_model
```

::: {.fragment}
> `exponentiate = TRUE` turns log-odds into **odds ratios** — much easier to interpret.
:::

---

## Visualize the odds ratios

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| output-location: slide
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 7
tidy_model |>
    filter(term != "(Intercept)") |>
    ggplot(aes(x = estimate, y = reorder(term, estimate))) +
    geom_pointrange(aes(xmin = conf.low, xmax = conf.high), alpha = 0.7) +
    geom_vline(xintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed", color = "red") +
    scale_x_log10() +
    labs(
        x = "Odds Ratio (95% CI)",
        y = NULL,
        title = "Predictors of Weapon Carrying at School"
    ) +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 13)
```

::: {.fragment}
> Predictors with CI **above 1** are associated with *more* weapon carrying. Below 1 = *less*. Crossing 1 = inconclusive.
:::

---

## Quick model-level summary with `glance()`

```{r}
#| echo: true
weapon_fit |> glance()
```

::: {.fragment}
> Returns AIC, BIC, deviance, log-likelihood — useful for comparing models.
:::

# 6️⃣ Predict: on the *test* set

## Predict and bind

```{r}
#| echo: true
predictions <-
    weapon_fit |>
    augment(new_data = analysis_test) |> # ⬅️ the test set!
    select(WeaponCarryingSchool, .pred_class, .pred_No, .pred_Yes)

predictions
```

::: {.fragment}
> `augment()` adds the predicted class and predicted **probabilities** to your data — no manual joining needed.
:::

::: {.fragment}
::: {.callout-warning}
## Always evaluate on the TEST set
The training metrics will look great because the model has *seen* that data. The test metrics tell you the truth.
:::
:::

# 7️⃣ Evaluate: metrics

## Confusion matrix

```{r}
#| echo: true
predictions |>
    conf_mat(truth = WeaponCarryingSchool, estimate = .pred_class)
```

```
          Truth
Prediction   No  Yes
       No  2298  187
       Yes   12   12
```

::: {.fragment}
::: {.incremental}
- **True Negatives** (correctly predicted "No"): 2298
- **True Positives** (correctly predicted "Yes"): 12
- **False Negatives** (missed "Yes"): 187 ⚠️
- **False Positives** (false alarms): 12
:::
:::

::: {.fragment}
> 👀 The model rarely predicts "Yes" — that's class imbalance biting back. We'll address it tomorrow with downsampling and tuning.
:::

---

## A `metric_set()` of metrics in one shot

```{r}
#| echo: true
weapon_metrics <- metric_set(
    accuracy,
    sensitivity,
    specificity,
    roc_auc
)

predictions |>
    weapon_metrics(
        truth = WeaponCarryingSchool,
        estimate = .pred_class,
        .pred_Yes, # the probability column for ROC
        event_level = "second" # "Yes" is the second level alphabetically
    )
```

::: {.fragment}
| Metric | What it tells you |
|--------|-------------------|
| **Accuracy** | % correct overall (misleading with imbalance) |
| **Sensitivity** | Of all true Yes, how many did we catch? |
| **Specificity** | Of all true No, how many did we correctly clear? |
| **ROC AUC** | How well the model **ranks** Yes vs No (0.5 = random, 1 = perfect) |
:::

---

## ROC curve

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| output-location: slide
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 7
predictions |>
    roc_curve(
        truth = WeaponCarryingSchool,
        .pred_Yes,
        event_level = "second"
    ) |>
    autoplot()
```

::: {.fragment}
> A curve hugging the **top-left** corner = a great model. A diagonal line = random guessing.
:::

# 🪄 The `last_fit()` Magic

## Steps 5 + 6 + 7 in one line ✨

`last_fit()` does it all: fits on the training set, predicts on the test set, and computes metrics.

```{r}
#| echo: true
final_results <-
    weapon_workflow |>
    last_fit(
        split = analysis_split,
        metrics = metric_set(accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, roc_auc)
    )

# Get the test metrics
final_results |> collect_metrics()

# Get the test predictions
final_results |> collect_predictions()
```

::: {.fragment}
::: {.callout-tip}
## Why `last_fit()` is your best friend
- ✅ Splits, recipes, fits, predicts, metrics — all in one object.
- ✅ Impossible to accidentally evaluate on the training set.
- ✅ Reproducible from a single command.
- ✅ The cleanest way to *finalize* your model after tuning.
:::
:::

# 🔁 A Taste of Resampling (Tomorrow's Topic)

## Why resample?

::: {.incremental}
- The test set is **sacred** — we can only look at it once at the end.
- But during model development we still need to estimate performance, compare models, and tune hyperparameters.
- **Solution:** carve up the **training set** into smaller "mini test sets" using **cross-validation**.
:::

---

## `vfold_cv()` — V-fold cross-validation

```{r}
#| echo: true
set.seed(1990)

analysis_folds <-
    vfold_cv(
        analysis_train,
        v = 5,
        strata = WeaponCarryingSchool
    )

analysis_folds
```

::: {.fragment}
> Splits the training set into **5 folds**. Each fold takes a turn being the "validation set" while the other 4 train. → 5 estimates of performance.
:::

---

## Other resampling flavors

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Bootstrapping
```{r}
#| echo: true
set.seed(1990)

bootstraps(analysis_train, times = 25)
```

Sample **with replacement** — useful for very small datasets.

### Leave-One-Out
```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false
# ⚠️ Don't actually run this on a 12k-row dataset — it would create 12k folds!
loo_cv(analysis_train)
```

Each observation is its own fold. Great for tiny data, **way too expensive** for big data like ours.

### Monte Carlo
```{r}
#| echo: true
mc_cv(analysis_train, prop = 0.75, times = 20)
```

Repeated random splits — flexible alternative to V-fold.

:::

::: {.fragment}
> 🚀 **Tomorrow** we'll feed `analysis_folds` into `tune_grid()` to pick the best Lasso penalty.
:::

- 🌐 [tidymodels.org](https://www.tidymodels.org/) — official site
- 🎯 [tidymodels Learn](https://www.tidymodels.org/learn/) — tutorials by level
- 📋 [Available models in `parsnip`](https://www.tidymodels.org/find/parsnip/) — 238+ engines
- 📊 [`yardstick` metric reference](https://yardstick.tidymodels.org/articles/metric-types.html)
- 🧪 [`recipes` step gallery](https://recipes.tidymodels.org/reference/index.html)
- 🎥 [Julia Silge's screencasts](https://www.youtube.com/@JuliaSilge) — tidymodels on real data, weekly
- 🤖 [`usemodels`](https://usemodels.tidymodels.org/) — auto-generates the recipe + workflow scaffold
